utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, Madam Witness. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Excellency. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since I don't have much time I would like to ask you to give yes or no answers to all questions that allow for that possibility. Of course, you are perfectly entitled to ask for more time as well, but I will try to be as expeditious as possible. You say that they did not go back to work. Persons who were close to you or persons you knew, were they called back to work? Did they receive IDs? And were they escorted?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you believe it if I were to tell that a person you know well was called back, given an escort, given an ID, and came all the way up until that person was arrested?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said -- actually, where was it that you were questioned when you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an office that was above the restaurant. That's the management building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say that that also happened in your rooms, the women's rooms?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Women slept in these rooms during the night. Not men, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there were no interrogations in these rooms?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were interrogations in these rooms where, as I've already said, we used to spend the night. During the day interrogations took place in those same rooms every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't only in the offices, as you said, but it was in these rooms too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are rooms and offices at the same time. That's where we spend our -- spent our nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, for instance, well, you said in -- now I'll tell you what case that was. In your statement, actually, of February 1995, on page 4, you said that some Zeljko, it's probably Meakic, told a guard that he could not drink when he was on duty.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that once a man came drunk. He wasn't even a guard. I don't know who he was. He came there drunk. He came into our room, the room where I was, because women were put into two rooms that were used for questioning detainees during the day. That's where women spent the night, but during the day they would go down to the restaurant every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yet another guard chased away some person who entered the premises unauthorised. Actually, pointed a gun at this person, Radenko Spiric?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You've confused this. That was in Trnopolje, that was not in Omarska, when Radenko Spiric prevented Zoran Zigic from entering the room where the women from Omarska were. This does not have to do with Omarska. That is Trnopolje. When we were transferred from Omarska to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have trouble hearing the witness. Could all microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have the reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you've completed your question, could you turn down your microphone. When we have a witness with the voice distortion, we have to do that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: that he entered a room where the women from Omarska were, where the women from Omarska were kept, and also that he pointed a rifle at him. Oh, yes, it is possible that that is where the women who had come from Omarska were kept. At any rate, this Spiric prevented someone who was trying to get close to these women. He stopped that by using a rifle.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained, it's Trnopolje, not Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said -- in your statement from February 1995 on page 15 and in your proof of testimony you said that someone had said to you, How come you're here? You were supposed to be indicted, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that was in Trnopolje. That is what the commander of the Trnopolje camp said, Slobodan Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether anybody had pardoned you and that was the reason why you were not indicted?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. No one said anything to me. No one communicated anything to me. I was just transferred, together with a few other women, from the Omarska camp to the Trnopolje camp. No one told me the reason why this was being done, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you were to have been pardoned as opposed to those who had been released without being pardoned, that means that you would have otherwise been indicted; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, you do know that much, don't you? Whoever is released without a pardon is not indicted whereas a person who is pardoned can no longer be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in normal situations, whereas these were extraordinary circumstances that really had nothing to do with any rules or regulations. The Criminal Code was not in force. The Law on Investigations, or criminal investigations, nothing. I never knew what it was that I was being accused of and why I was kept at the Omarska camp for so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's not go through all of this yet again, but did they not tell you that you were well known for your extremism and that you were meeting with a group that was also accused of extremism?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one has said that to me, that I was well known for my extremism. When I was questioned in the Omarska camp, two investigators, Nenad Babic and Nenad Tomcic, asked me where I met people, who I met, what we talked about during our encounters when I would sit with different persons. This was simply their information that they were presenting to me. However, they had not told me of any indictment issued against me or that I was a suspect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could you be kind enough to come closer to the microphone so that interpreters can follow you better. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of February 1995, on page 14, you said that two persons were taken away and that afterwards you never saw these people. This sentence is repeated in the case of many witnesses, yourself included. They were taken out and we no -- never saw them again, words to that effect. Are you trying to suggest something by saying that, or are you aware of the fact that persons were being released even before the 3rd of August, in succession. As soon as a person is proven innocent, then this person would be released, allowed to go home?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at the Omarska concentration camp, to the best of my recollection, it was only once that one group of detainees was transferred to Trnopolje. At least that's what the camp guards were saying. Along with the other women, I had work obligation; namely, at the restaurant, or, rather, the camp cafeteria. I was handing food out to the detainees, this single meal that was distributed there. Very often I would notice that some people no longer came to get that single meal. When they would walk towards the restaurant, they would have to walk through a group of guards who would beat them using different objects. So they actually avoided coming to the cafeteria for that meal in order to avoid any kind of physical abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, the Prosecutor will ask you about that. With all due respect, please do not expand on this. Just answer my questions. So you say if you do not see someone there for lunch, you think that something bad happened to that person; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That that person was no longer there. Our suspicions were that such a person was killed during the night and that this person could be found on those heaps of dead bodies on the lawn in front of the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. We are going to prove that what are you saying is not correct. However, let us leave it aside now. Were there releases, individual releases, when a person was proven innocent? Would such a person be released, allowed to go home, not to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4639, could we please have that in e-court. Testimony before this Court. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall the Chamber move into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, this testimony and your showbiz appearance in the media, is that also part of your struggle against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't understand you. What do you mean against the Serbs? I don't lump people together. I'm talking about bad people. The fact that they happened to be Serbs, it's not my fault. What kind of struggle do you think I'm waging against the Serbs? I still have Serb friends, nice people who have full understanding about what I have gone through. There's no stigmatisation at all. It's not even that I have a need to talk about what happened. It's just that I can't forget it. Five of my colleagues and friends were killed in Omarska, my work colleagues. Exhumations and visits to mass graves have become an integral part of my life. Where did you get this impression that I am a person trying to stigmatise a whole people, a whole community? Never, ever, have I ever displayed any hatred towards the people as a whole. Never said a word about it in any interview. I just blame people who committed crimes regardless of their ethnicity, and I accept that members of other ethnic communities also committed crimes. Let Serbs and Croats also speak about their experiences as victims, and I will support them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask about her investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. No. We go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now that the cross-examination is over, Ms. Edgerton, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually do, Your Honour, if I may. And I think I can do it in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, the newspaper article that Dr. Karadzic showed you and you commented on at page 16, lines 10 and 11 of this transcript, you have actually seen that newspaper article before, when testifying at this Tribunal, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your comments relating to that newspaper article are reproduced in the statement that was read back to you in Sarajevo, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one further question. At page 6 of today's transcript, lines 16 to 21, Dr. Karadzic asked you: "So you say if you do not someone there for lunch, you think that something bad happened to that person; right?"

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your response was: "Yes. That that person was no longer there. Our suspicions were that such a person was killed during the night and this person would be found on those heaps of dead bodies on the lawn in front of the 'White House.'" Do you remember that? I'm sorry, you have to articulate your answer.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I repeat? I was saying when somebody doesn't show up, when one of the inmates, the prisoners, failed to show up at the refectory for a meal, then we started to think that something bad had happened. And then the next morning, when we come from our rooms to the refectory and we see heaps of bodies on the lawn outside, sometimes we were able to recognise by the clothes who it was because people wore the same clothes throughout their imprisonment there. They continued wearing the clothes they were brought in. And that's why I said there was always this suspicion that somebody who had not shown up for a meal had come to a bad end and some of these suspicions -- these suspicions were usually justified. These people were, for the most part, eventually found in mass graves and later reburied.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I not ask a question but address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- were you minded to tender that interview into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both the interview and this publication from the Internet, this human rights thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection to the admission of those two documents, Ms. Edgerton, under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With the tag, with respect to the publication from the Internet, this human rights thing, that the only accurate information you had about the source of that document came from the Prosecution and it's not put into any sort of context so that Your Honours were able to assess the forum in which the discussion took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no problem with the interview, especially given that it's referred to in the witness's amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Those two will be admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 1D4489 will be Exhibit D1819, under seal. And 65 ter number 1D4482 will be Exhibit D1820, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have further matters to address the Chamber in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does not relate only to the witness but it has to do with the heaps of dead bodies. The investigators Drasko Zec, Milenko Tomic and Zivko Dragosavljevic are still alive and active today. Dragosavljevic was president of the court after the war. Now he owns a law office, and so do Zec and Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think it's time to hear such a submission from you in the presence of the witness. Would you agree, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure -- if you maybe would let him finish because I'm not sure what his objective is, but he usually has a pretty good objective. So if you can let him finish with his point, I think maybe it would become more clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask the Chamber to ask

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Have these people been prosecuted for these heaps of dead bodies that she refers to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was for you to put that question in your cross-examination. That concludes your evidence, Madam Witness. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, that concludes your evidence in real terms. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give your testimony. And now you are free to go. We'll rise all together. This time we'll take a break for half an hour, and resume at ten to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I'd like to introduce Nathalie Dauphin, who is a legal intern with our Defence team who will be joining us for this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And next, if we could go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, it is you, Mr. Zec. Or Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next Prosecution witness, Mr. President, is Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Mevludin Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to ask you to confirm a few background details before we get into other questions. First, is it correct that you were born in the Vlasenica area but raised in the Prijedor municipality, more specifically in the Trnopolje area, since you were a young child?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You attended university in Tuzla and served in the JNA in Serbia in an artillery unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were a founding member of the SDA Party in 1990 and were elected in the 1990 elections to the republic assembly of the chamber of municipalities as the Prijedor representative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The Prijedor representative in the council of municipalities of the republic parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you also attend municipal assembly meetings in Prijedor and split your time between Sarajevo and Prijedor from the time of the election until 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I attended the sessions of the republic parliament without fail, and I also attended the municipal assembly sessions in Prijedor when I was able to, when I was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which party won the most seats in the November 1990 elections in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The Party for Democratic Action, the SDA, won the most seats, and the second-ranking party was the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to -- let me ask you quickly. And did the -- did the members of the SDA assume leading positions in the municipality in accordance with the electoral results; and did SDS members also assume numbers of significant positions in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Important positions were divided according to electoral results and in keeping with an inter-party agreement that had been made earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I'm going to be bringing your attention soon to the assumption of exclusive power in the municipality by the Serbian authorities at the end of April 1992, as well as the events that followed. But I first wanted to ask you if you and other members of the SDA were able to identify indications between the time of the election and the end of April 1992 that such events were developing or imminent; and, if so, if you could tell us what those were?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In chronology, there were several things that had been differently interpreted by different parties, but we were also able to observe some practical moves by the SDS that were contrary to the inter-party agreement, that were contrary to constitutional conduct, followed by open conflicts within the institutions of power. We lived in an atmosphere where influences from the neighbouring countries also affected our area, our region. The prevailing Serbian policy at the time applied in identical form in neighbouring countries, which also complicated the social and political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say "neighbouring country" do you have a particular neighbouring country in mind in terms of the political policy that began to be applied in identical form?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost I mean Croatia where conflicts had already started because Croatia had already seceded and declared its independence. And then the people in one part of its territory mounted an insurgency. However, the engine of that policy was located in Serbia which was obvious from the propaganda instruments. Another decisive factor in all these events was the Yugoslav Army, which was increasingly becoming a Serb-controlled army, an army controlled by what remained of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You referred to the actions of one part of the territory of Croatia taking -- declaring independence and taking -- being involved in conflict with the other. Did -- in Bosnia, to what extent were you able to identify similar steps within the context of the unfolding events between the election and the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The events that began to unfold in Bosnia and Herzegovina and especially the Bosnian Krajina were a mirror image of what was going on and what had already happened in the Knin Krajina. It was not just a similarity, an analogy, but also the newly formed Serbian forces in the Knin Krajina crossed over from Croatia, and their military forces entered Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were some Serbs from Prijedor who joined the Martic militia in Croatia as volunteers, and after individual operations, they would return to Prijedor and continue to live there. And you were able to see them around town, in bars, wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you become familiar with the process of -- termed "regionalisation" in the Bosnian Krajina in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: As early as 1991, the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, or, rather, its representatives, demanded a regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina although that regionalisation already existed. However, it did not suit their plans because their aspiration was for regionalisation to be ethnic based and that was not possible either by the law or by the constitution. We realised very early on that they actually wanted to create Serb regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina not unlike the Serb Autonomous Region in Croatia, and the events that unfolded in quick succession from that point on made their intentions quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also earlier mentioned propaganda and propaganda instruments. What were you referring to by that, in the context of events developing in 1991 and 1992, leading to the end of April 1992, with the assumption of power by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That propaganda had a certain history before the war. It had gone on for a couple of years before the war, but then it intensified. It emanated from Serbia, and its inevitable consequence and its purpose was to affect the strong traditions of peaceful co-existence in our country. The propaganda was based on fueling fears from new suffering. However, since they did not have enough instruments in terms of propaganda, they decided to take up arms, take over the TV repeaters that were until then not under their control and to broadcast their own programmes. That's what happened to the TV repeater at Lisina already in the middle of 1991. That takeover meant the switching off of programmes that were not produced in Serbia or in Banja Luka or some other Serb region. From that moment on, you could not follow any other programme via that transmitter. The topics they covered and the programmes they broadcast was reviving memories of the Second World War, mass graves, the threats to the Serbian people, the suffering of Serbs in Croatia, and, of course, later, news from the war in Croatia. Throughout this time, nothing positive could be heard about any other ethnic community. You could only hear these programmes about conspiracy against the Serb people, victory at the front line and so on. This exerted additional psychological pressure on the non-Serb population but it also raised fear among the non-Serb population and tensions were heightened. The aim was to mobilise all of the Serb people for what had obviously been planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you begin to hear proposals for or demands for ethnic separation by the SDS, either at the republic level, or the municipality level, or both?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the SDS offered this at the level of the republic when discussing it with officials from other parties. All of us in Bosnia knew full well what that meant and we realised that this could not be achieved and also that it was unnecessary to begin with. However, our positions were not taken into account at all. The SDS justified all of this in a most unconvincing way by referring to this wish to have the Serb people remain within Yugoslavia. However, there was something else behind all of that. A few months later, these claims were made in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor and a proposal was made to divide Prijedor into two municipalities, that institutions be divided along ethnic lines. Of course, that could not be considered at all. That was not provided for by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the law that was in force. Sometime after that, we realised what had preceded all of that. We realised what the proposal was when "Kozarski Vjesnik," the official newspaper of Prijedor, ran an article where the SDS openly stated that over 70 per cent of the territory of Prijedor was considered to be Serb territory. Also, they said that the factories, the national park, the forests, the stadium, the agricultural farms, all of that which was jointly owned all of a sudden was considered to be Serb property only. Only some very small farms were marked as Muslim and Croat. The message was quite clear. That message had nothing whatsoever to do with any law or the constitution itself. It was a major reason for this incredible fear that was sown among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During that same period, 1991 through early 1992, did you also learn anything about the arming of the Serb -- Serbian population of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that we only heard about that. We also had an opportunity of seeing it. In our party, we received reports several times. That also happened in the village that I lived in. The army used helicopters to transport weapons to two locations and then they divided these weapons among the Serbs, and literally in the middle of the road at midday, in front of the cultural centre, they took weapons out of a truck and gave these weapons to the people who were asked to come there and take them. In our talks with our colleagues who were SDS officials in the municipality, we brought this up, but they all denied that kind of thing having happened. For example, specifically, when the helicopter landed near my village, the neighbours explained this by saying that purportedly a soldier from that village was in that helicopter and they wanted to stop and have coffee at his house. People saw the boxes with ammunition, but they denied that there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You spoke about the fears felt by the non-Serb population. In the weeks immediately preceding April 29th and 30th, did the SDA or HDZ or other parties propose measures to ease the fears and ease the tensions to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Several times we made proposals to the SDS. We beseeched them, saying that wherever people felt threatened by another ethnic community, we should establish joint patrols consisting of persons of different ethnic backgrounds who would be on guard duty during the night and that way there would be no reason to have any kind of fear on either side. I have to point something out. In some locations, this was an initiative that came from the population itself, that they have this joint guard duty during the night so that some troops would not come from elsewhere and create a problem. The SDS opposed that, and a few days later, at three locations - I know that for sure - where there were these joint guards, the local SDS ordered that the Serbs withdraw from these joint patrols. We know that for sure because in the village where I lived, we had talks to that effect. We asked people to stay, but the man said very openly, We have received our orders to withdraw, and our order was that everyone should guard his own house. From that moment onwards, we lost yet another hope that we would manage to ease the fears and tensions in Prijedor. On one occasion, we pleaded with the SDS. We said that if they thought that the army was threatened along roads, that we established mixed groups consisting of soldiers and locals. However, that was resolutely rejected. That is to say, that any gesture that meant any kind of interethnic cooperation was nipped in the bud, wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you briefly about the nature of the parties and their organisational structure. With respect to the SDA first, was it a hierarchical organisation where instructions from the top were passed on to lower levels and obliged to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In principle, that is how all parties functioned in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what I can assert, as far as the SDA is concerned. The top of the party is the president. Then there was an Executive Board of the party. There was a Main Board. All of that was at the level of the state. And then at lower levels there were party centres. That is to say, there were regional committees headed by a president, and at municipal level there were Municipal Boards headed by their respective presidents. That was the hierarchy. All important decisions were made from top to bottom. They were carried out at lower levels. Initiatives could be launched from the grass roots, but decisions were made at top level and then take further down. Only decisions of local importance, not of republican importance, could be made at local level. However, the top leadership of the party needed to approve that as well. Other parties, as far as I know, functioned in accordance with the same principle. However, their main or executive bodies sometimes had a different name. Some parties had a Presidency, others had an Executive Board. They all had a Main Board. Most of them had regional boards. And they all had Municipal Boards, if they had their party organised at municipal level as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say that other parties, as far as you know, functioned in accordance with the same principle. Specifically with respect to the SDS --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a problem with the volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please wait until our usher can assist you. Let us see how the usher can assist you. Is the volume too loud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's fine. Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let us proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was about to ask the following, Mr. Sejmenovic. You said that other parties, as far as you knew, functioned in accordance with the same principle. I wanted to ask you specifically with respect to the SDS, was that understanding based on your dealings with local and republic SDS officials and your observations of their interactions and their policies?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The SDS, like other parties, had a president, a Main Board. And now did they have a Presidency? Were these main people around the president called the Presidency or something else but they did exist at any rate. So basically it was a Presidency. They certainly had a Main Board. At local level, they had a president. They had Municipal Boards and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, more specifically, were you able to determine whether policies and instructions emanated at the top and were issued to the lower levels and expected to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, what is it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is not a leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with -- specifically, Mr. Sejmenovic, with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did we have the answer to the previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I heard the answer. I didn't look at the transcript actually. Yes. The transcript indicates the witness answering, of course, and then the objection, the comment, objection by Mr. Karadzic is attributed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sejmenovic, with respect to the positions on ethnic separation, did you see any difference in the position taken at the republic level of the SDS and the position taken at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There was no difference. However, in terms of practical behaviour, in Prijedor, this ethnic division went more slowly than requested by the top echelons of the SDS. I heard about that from Srdja Srdic who was a member of parliament from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, I indicated I wanted to take you to the events of April 29th and 30th and ask you about that. When did you become aware of -- first of all, can you tell us what happened on April 29th or April 30th and how you became aware of it, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just intervene on the transcript. The witness did not say that Srdja Srdic was a member of a paramilitary. He said that he was a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is exactly what we said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is reflected as a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until my objection it said "paramilitary."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's a magic -- let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I had asked you if you to tell the Court what happened on April 29th and 30th in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 20th of April, including the 29th of April, we were involved in talks with the SDS, and we tried to establish cooperation at any level or in any way, with a view to convincing the SDS that we did not have any hidden intentions whatsoever. What surprised us a day or two before that was something very serious. In "Kozarski Vjesnik," a long article appeared where it said that Serbs in Prijedor were about to be massacred. That that was being prepared. People asked for an explanation. Why was the atmosphere being poisoned to that extent? There is no reason whatsoever. However, something else happened during the night. Between 1.00 a.m. and 5.00 a.m., the entire town was taken by military means. By weapons, I mean. All institutions, all vital facilities, patrols, sniper nests, machine-gun nests, sandbags, ramps, check-points, throughout the municipality around Prijedor in several different locations. It was amazing that all of that was done within those four or five hours. The population was totally unaware of what was going on. In the morning when people went to town, when they were leaving their homes, as they were going to work, they saw soldiers and policemen all over the place and they saw them behind sandbags, with rifles pointed at them. That morning, unaware what was going on, I had set out to Prijedor. After take -- I mean, I took the bus. And after having been on the bus for about 2 kilometres, soldiers stopped the bus and checked the IDs of all who were on that bus. And only then I saw the sandbags and the patrols and check-points. It was quite clear to me that something extraordinary had happened. However, what had actually happened, I found out only when I arrived Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, Mr. Sejmenovic, when you speak about soldiers and policemen with rifles and behind sandbags, are you speaking about soldiers and policemen of a particular ethnicity and associated with any particular group?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That was all the Serbian army and Serbian policemen. Prijedor is a small town, and other people, the non-Serbs who were very confused by these events and who came to the party to ask for information, knew most of these men. And I also met some of my colleagues who were now carrying rifles in some places. They were checking people's IDs. I even tried to ask one of them what that was all about. Dragan, what is this? What is happening? He didn't want to tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you what happened in the aftermath of this takeover by the Serbian authorities to the non-Serb population. So, first of all, let me ask you, let me focus on official institutions. Can you tell the Court what the impact was on non-Serb officials in Prijedor, including -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning hours of that day, the new authorities which had taken over power began broadcasting messages over the radio and they made clear what was happening. What was happening on the ground was this: The non-Serbs who were going to work that morning were sent back from the gates of their factories or institutions where they were employed. No non-Serb could enter the municipal building. They were all sent back, including the chief of the municipality. As for the payment operation service, nobody could enter it as well. No one could enter the banks. The non-Serbian population was thrown out of most important enterprises, institutions, and organs of power. No one was allowed entry. The only place where people requested information about what was going on was the party, the SDA. But there they could not obtain any information because the SDS did not respond to the calls of the SDA officials who were calling them, asking for an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what about the non-Serb members of the police?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the police, we know that because our official who was delegated by the SDA, Hasan Talundzic, who was the chief, informed us that, during the night, they were disarmed. I mean, the policemen who were non-Serbs. They were sent back from the entrance or they were thrown out of the police station if they happened to have been there. Some of them were promised that they would still be employed if they signed a declaration of loyalty. He also informed us that a man tried to sign this statement of loyalty but he was not allowed to do that. Four or five days later we also received information that one inspector had signed this statement of loyalty but he was dismissed from his position anyway. After a few days, non-Serb teachers were also dismissed from schools, most of them. On the first day, movement outside the territory of Prijedor municipality was prohibited, and a few days later, moving towards the town of Prijedor from the non-Serb populated areas was also prohibited. What followed later on were power cuts and telephone lines were also cut in the non-Serb populated areas. Simultaneously, with the -- these steps taken by the new authorities, there were propaganda statements which were broadcast and which talked about arming, the threats against Serbs, about the Green Berets which reported they intended to take over power in Prijedor and this was broadcast for days. And at the same time, on many occasions one could hear the sentence that without a single shot they had managed to take over the power. How, if there had been these thousands of Green Berets? However, at the time, the propaganda was actually necessary for the Serbian population so that they could more easily face the events that would follow a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If can I quickly call up 65 ter 05445.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, this is a document dated 11 May 1992 from the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff to the president of the municipality generally. If I could ask you quickly to look at the second provision in item 4.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you zoom in a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that sufficient or can we -- perhaps we can zoom in a bit more. Which indicates that: "Only person who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina can be placed in the management positions in enterprises." I wanted to ask you if that was consistent with what happened in Prijedor with respect to dismissals of non-Serbs from management positions. And, if you can tell us, any other positions.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. This is precisely how the situation in Prijedor developed. In accordance with the positions which are formulated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me to say that it was not just those who were in management positions but even labourers were sent away from factories sometime after this. I mean, labourers who were non-Serbs by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3694, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, you spoke about the events that followed the takeover. These increasing steps against the non-Serb population. The allegations of threats against the Serbs and so on. Did the SDA and officials, non-Serb officials in Prijedor, attempt to meet with the SDS in an effort to address these restrictions and these allegations and somehow ameliorate the situation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There were many attempts on the first two or three days. No one from the SDS did not want to respond to a call from anyone from the SDA. After two or three days, supposedly not as representatives of the party but privately some people would meet with others but that yielded no results. We kept asking and begging and we managed to beg from Mr. Miskovic, who was the president of the SDS, to meet with us and to try to find a solution for the situation that had arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We met in the premises of the SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you don't have to identify everyone, but who came on behalf of the SDA or HDZ or the non-Serb representatives?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Several officials of SDA came. We also expected that the president of the SDS would be there, as well as some of the top officials. However, once we got there, to his room, the SDS did not want to begin the meeting. The president of the SDS, Miskovic, said that the commander of the 5th Kozarac Brigade, Arsic, and the commander of the Prijedor garrison, Zeljaja, had to attend the meeting. Some persons were present whom I had not known up until then. And there was also a man called Slobodan Kuruzovic. I later saw that he was the camp warden of Trnopolje. The meeting only began when the military commanders arrived and two or three other persons who accompanied them. The commanders then introduced them as security officers. We hoped that these talks would be fruitful. We had a wish and a mild hope that perhaps we might reach some sort of an agreement. On the other hand, though, it all turned into a game. They first joked. Then they began very serious talks. They accused us of wanting to have war in Prijedor. And in the end, they gave us an ultimatum, to which we could not respond. We could not do what they asked us to do and they knew that it was impossible for us to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One quick question: You mentioned Slobodan Kuruzovic. Was he an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was one of the officials but I don't know precisely what position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Arsic was the commander of the 5th Kozarac Brigade, and Zeljaja, the commander of the Prijedor garrison. Just to clarify, did you understand them to be members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Certainly. The Prijedor garrison existed earlier. And the 5th Kozara Brigade, which was huge, had withdrawn its forces from Croatia and stationed them in Prijedor. These forces were commanded by Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you and the other members of the SDA do your best to persuade the SDS members and Zeljaja and Arsic, as you told us here, that you had no interest in or did not desire war in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We tried everything. Everything that reason can do. However, Your Honours, these were talks where, on one side, you had people with rockets, guns, tanks, aircraft, and who told you that. That group accused us, who had no army to oppose them at all, this group accused us of wanting war. And then they accused us and set conditions which were like an ultimatum, that within 48 hours, we had to surrender several thousand pieces of weaponry, which we didn't have. After they told us that with a short deadline we had to surrender the weapons, we tried to explain. Medunjanin said, Look here, people, how can we do that when we don't have it? Commander Zeljaja just said, That's your problem. If you do not do that, I will raze Kozarac to the ground. He repeated twice this sentence, I shall raze Kozarac to the ground. Repeated attempt to convince them because we begged them on that occasion as well to come with us so that we could show them, so that we could secure the roads together. Nothing helped. They refused to hold any further talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to tell any difference between the positions taken by Arsic and Zeljaja and the SDS officials present?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I used the expression that they were playing with us. One of the arguments which supports the position that they were really playing with us were the jokes that they were making which were not funny at all. But another argument was that one of the security men claimed that we had 7.000 rifles in Kozarac. Another one claimed that we had 11.500 in the territory of the municipality. Zeljaja said that, as far as I can remember, that we needed to return 5.000 within 48 hours. So not unanimous, but all the figures were far from reality. There was just legitimate Territorial Defence in Kozarac. It was very poorly armed, and there was nothing else except that. Around Kozarac, there were several artillery batteries which had ammunition, and they also had their barrels turned towards non-Serb populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. Just a couple of quick follow-up questions, first of all, although it may be clear in context, the artillery batteries to which you referred which had their barrels turned towards non-Serb populated areas belonged to who?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: They belonged to the Serbian forces or the Serbian army, as the commanders called this army. And previously, it had been the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. And all the materiel actually belonged to the 5th Kozara Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And notwithstanding the difference in the claimed number of weapons held by the Muslims, by various people at the meeting, I had asked you whether Zeljaja and Arsic took different positions generally with regard to the ultimatum and with regard to the attitude towards the non-Serb population than the SDS or took the same positions, and I wanted you to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: They took identical position. Their position was identical. And as for the weapons, they knew and they had realistic assessments, and their conditions, their request that such and such a number of barrels, the thousands of barrels needed to be returned, that was part of their intention to give them an ultimatum that we could not respond to. They knew that the area was not armed in the military sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in the face of this meeting and all you've described, did you and other members of the SDA meet with the local non-Serb leaders of Prijedor, in particular -- particularly Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Several meetings were held and attempts at meetings, because it was no longer easy to go to Prijedor. You had to take country roads so as to avoid military patrols and several meetings were held in Kozarac, which I attended. After the meeting that we just talked about, we went back to Kozarac and held a meeting there. It was attended by officials of the Territorial Defence, the local communes, the local police. I was there as a member of the republican assembly. And we decided to inform the people about the ultimatum we had been given, and we decided to hold a rally to invite the citizens to attend so that we would decide what we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before I go on to that, speaking of the non-Serb members of the local TO and police, can you tell the Court how the SDS members and Zeljaja and Arsic referred to the local TO members and police during that meeting you described?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: They called them all the Green Berets. Whatever was not the Serbian army were the Green Berets for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at the meeting that you indicated you decided to hold, and at the various meetings that were held, can you tell us what the -- the gist of the efforts were and the focus was at -- at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Most of these meetings were focussed on attempts to try and find a way to cooperate with the SDS and this army and the police, regardless of their ultimatum both at the level of the Prijedor municipality and the level of Banja Luka, which was the then Krajina region which they had established. We tried to find personal, private connections. Whoever had any sort of contact, we tried to use it so that we could really show the armed side that there was no reason for all this whatsoever. However, all these attempts were fruitless. At the same time we were living in great fear because everything that was going on in the neighbouring towns told us that the same scenario was being prepared for us, just like in Sanski Most, in Bosanski Novi, and in some other towns in the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did -- were any efforts made to put some kind of defence in place?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... a very short time we tried to expand and reinforce the Territorial Defence. We called on people to place themselves at the disposal to the Territorial Defence. It was the Territorial Defence which called on the people to place themselves at its disposal. If they possessed any weapons, that the weapons should be listed, and that some sort of structure should be established, in order to prevent the population in non-Serb populated areas in Kozarac and surrounding areas, from being massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were people conscripted or obliged to make themselves available to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. There was no conscription because there was no fundamental condition. You cannot mobilise anything if you don't know who you can mobilise. First of all, we needed to establish how many people wished to place themselves at the disposal of the Territorial Defence. It was completely voluntarily. We made the lists, and the list did not only include non-Serbs, not just Bosniaks or Muslims. There were others as well. At the Territorial Defence Staff in Kozarac, there were two Serbian gentlemen. Unfortunately, a day or two before the attack, they left. The attempt to organise Territorial Defence, to reinforce it in terms of establishment, was something that we could not finish. We did not have the personnel we needed. We did not have the funds, the materiel. We did not have appropriate communication means. We did not have telecommunication equipment in -- that would enable us to establish appropriate contacts. We did not have fuel. And those who had placed themselves at the disposal of the Territorial Defence and who wished to be included in these lists could not be used. Most of them. Either because of their age or because they possessed no weapons whatsoever, or they had something that they had made themselves or they had antiquated weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What -- what sort -- first of all, how large was the existing TO before this process began? And I just mean in general terms. Large or small?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It was very small. I can give you approximate numbers. With a population of 30.000, the TO had perhaps 50 to 100 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what kind of weaponry did the TO have before this process began; and, if it didn't have much, why not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It had no weapons because the year before, the Yugoslav army took the weapons away from the Territorial Defence, stored it in their depots, and then at the request of the republican leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina they returned only a small part of the weaponry. But even the part they returned was obsolete, mainly rifles from the Second World War, the so-called M48 rifles, and just a few automatic rifles here and there [as interpreted], in symbolic amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now you spoke about --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? And the witness said: "A few other things here and there," which is not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see it in the transcript, but maybe we're talking about something else. But I know that sometimes the transcribers have to catch up or revise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for safety, shall we ask the witness to repeat his last answer, if he could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said mainly rifles from World War II, M48, a few automatic weapons, and a few other things here and there. I can clarify in order not to leave any issues outstanding. Along with those rifles, local TO units had a small number of RPGs each. Those were projectiles that are screwed onto the barrel of a rifle to fire grenades. I don't know of any other weapons they had. They certainly had no artillery, at least no -- not in the local communes that I had occasion to visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, you spoke about the artillery positions and about the mounting fears of an attack on the non-Serb populated areas, including Kozarac. Was there ultimately an attack on Kozarac by the Bosnian Serb forces; and, if so, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of May. There was an all-out attack on Kozarac with artillery shelling from several directions using a variety of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before I ask you about the details of that attack, had there been any shelling of non-Serb populated areas by the Bosnian Serb forces before the 24th and the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Two days before, that is to say, on the 22nd, a place called Hambarine was shelled, and the purported reason for the shelling was that a member of the Territorial Defence had shot at a vehicle carrying Serb troops. That's what we heard on the radio. Then followed an artillery attack, and that part of Hambarine was burned down completely. You could easily hear the explosions and a huge fire in that area. We could watch it from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have, for reasons of principle, to object to the question by Mr. Tieger where he defines the forces of the Bosnian Serbs. We have still not established what Bosnian Serb forces are. At that time, it was the JNA and its reservists were killed in Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at that time it was not the JNA, because the JNA had decided a few days earlier to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina and withdrew. We welcomed the news because it gave us a flicker of hope that, perhaps, peace would prevail there. However, the JNA did not withdraw. They just changed their name. The officers called themselves the Serb army, and the troop numbers increased even more in the area of Prijedor several days after the federal decision to pull the JNA out of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I will ask you about the forces you observed in Kozarac. But let me ask you as a predicate question whether you were able personally to observe the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I set out to go to Kozarac and the closest I was able to come to the area that was shelled was about 400 metres. I couldn't go any further because 155-millimetre Howitzers were firing into that area. The explosions were horrific. I did my compulsory military service in the artillery and I had one target practice using live rounds and I know what it means. I waited for about an hour at that point. However, the shelling continued. I returned to Trnopolje. The shelling still continued into the night, the whole night, and the whole day the next day. And it stopped only late the next day. I went there again briefly before the end of the shelling. The Serb infantry advanced and started burning houses at the entrance to the place. The houses were burning. Flames were reaching into the sky, and all we were able to see in the dark and in the light of the flames were people running to and fro, people falling. Some people burnt down in the burning houses. Some managed to escape, and those who managed to escape told us about what was going on and how it had started. They said, these people said, that the people burning down houses were using some special bombs because the house is set ablaze in a split second. After that, the fire and the shelling stopped. The military action stopped. Columns of refugees started fleeing, but the Serb infantry also advanced, driving people out and killing people in villages if they were stragglers, if they hadn't managed to escape. That situation continued and repeated itself around Trnopolje and in Trnopolje itself. And because of the particular vantage point I had in some of these situations, I was able to see it all with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask first before I ask you about your observations about what happened to some of the villages in the area. If you can indicate to the Court what happened to the people from Kozarac after the events you described, whether any distinction -- whether -- whether they went to a particular place, whether they were taken to a particular place, whether any distinction was made between portions of the population? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Everyone, men and even some older boys, were taken to the camp. Women and children were grouped in Trnopolje or in some places where groups of refugees had gathered. In the areas where there was a concentration of refugees, the army came several days later and killed a number of people there. And those who found shelter in those areas of large refugee concentrations were deported to other areas, and if they were men, they were deported to concentration camps, such as Omarska. Approximately a month later, there was no one and nothing left there. Not even birds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And forgive me for these clarifications, because I appreciate that you may find them implicit in your evidence. But when you say "everyone, men and even older boys, were taken to the camp," who or what groups took them into the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to protest again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say "boys." And Mr. Tieger is putting words in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say "boys." Older men and also boys, minors. And I saw personally several examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 25 in the previous page the witness said: "Even some older boys." Let's proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Witness, was: Who was it that took those men and boys to the camps?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: They were taken by soldiers who arrived in groups, fired, and then rounded up men. These soldiers wore a variety of uniforms. In the specific place where I watched all of this, from beginning to end, several soldiers had the Martic militia uniforms on. Others wore JNA uniforms. Yet others wore the uniforms of the 5th Kozara Brigade. Some wore pieces of uniform combined with civilian clothing, such as jeans with a camouflage blouse and sneakers on his feet. One of the operations was supported by a police APC. Some operations involved tanks. At one point I was very close to the passing group and I was able to overhear a bit of conversation among them. And from what I heard, I knew straight away that some of those soldiers were not from our area. They were not from Bosnian Krajina, and they were not even from Bosnia-Herzegovina, because some of them wore -- spoke typical Serbian from Serbia proper. A semi-uniformed person in that group said in -- in a bit of conversation that I managed to overhear, that he hailed from Banja Luka. He didn't say exactly, I am from Banja Luka. He said, It's better for me to come from Banja Luka here for a couple of days than to work a whole month. It pays better. That's how I understood that he is from Banja Luka, that he lives and works there, and then he comes for three-, four-day stints, and that he finds it more lucrative, more profitable. That was my inference from what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were all these groups operating together; and were these either Serbs from Serbia proper, as you indicated, or Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There were both kinds. But they were doing an identical job following the same procedure that had the same consequences. When I say procedure, I say that because I noticed that they approached these operations in the same way. First, they surround a hamlet, they open fire from all directions. They keep approaching the houses while firing. They get the men out of the houses, they line them up, and they take them towards vehicles, because in some cases vehicles had been prepared in advance. Otherwise, they would take them on foot towards Kozarac or towards Trnopolje. I learned later on that it was in fact in the direction of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now just to clarify, during this period of time while you were observing the things you described, were you walking around freely or were you in hiding?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no freedom of movement whatsoever. Only people who were running away in the convoys were free to move within the convoy. All around, there were troops, robbers, looters. There was shooting all around. Men carrying weapons went -- approached the convoys and started shooting and killed people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let's just clear it up. He did not say that only in the convoys they had freedom of movement but within the refugee groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within an area where the convoy of refugee was, between one group and another. If you want me to be precise, it's a diameter of about 300, 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A couple of quick questions. First of all, you referred to looting. Are you referring to random acts of looting or more organised forms of looting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The first day or two I thought they were random. And then I realised they were organised. I would see a big lorry arrive. I would see that amounts of property were collected in one place, and every three or four days it would be taken away by that lorry towards Kozarac. And then the lorry would come back. One group of looters or, rather, soldiers would be collecting refrigerators. Others would be collecting stoves and cookers. In fact, there was some sorting involved in their looting. And sometime later, I was able to see two large collection points for this looted property and I saw also a large meadow filled with refrigerators, perhaps thousands and thousands of refrigerators. And another field that I saw was filled with stoves using solid fuel. Very neatly lined, and I had no doubt that it was property looted from the area of Prijedor, from Kozarac, Hambarine, and other non-Serb places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, were you in fear of apprehension and were you in hiding during this time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, I was. I was hiding. I was hiding from everyone, from the Serb troops, the police, anyone Serb in uniform. But I also kept away from non-Serbs because I thought they would be more fearful, knowing that I was close by, and I didn't want them to suffer any consequences in case I was apprehended just because they had been with me or close to me, and that was why I stayed completely alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that because you were a political figure, political leader?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Serb forces were searching for surviving SDA officials, officials of opposition parties, managers, directors of big companies, and we were called Green Berets, Ustashas, Mujahedins, and all the other names. And we were the first on their search list after the occupation. I was aware of that, and that's why I decided to stay and to hide alone. I know of one case when some non-Serbs, fearing for their own safety and lives, drove out my mother from the house where she was hiding and turned her over to the Serb military forces. Through an unbelievable combination of circumstances, she survived, and I learned of it in good time. And lest I found myself in the same situation, or caused someone else to find themselves in that situation, I decided to hide alone, and I was making plans as to where to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You referred to the surviving SDA officials, managers, et cetera. Can you tell the Court what happened to most of the SDA and HDZ political leaders in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, almost everyone was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we do that, since Ms. Sutherland is here, in relation to the point you raised at the end of the hearing yesterday, you stated that there are security concerns on matters which are not normally dealt with in confidential filings, in addition to the addresses of witnesses. It's not clear, so if you could expand on that, if necessary, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think it is necessary. What I meant was that the witness's actual address was contained -- not only the country where he was residing but the address and also matters relating to issues of security concerns that the witness has or had at that time, and those sorts of issues would normally be dealt with in a confidential filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could be more specific as to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I don't have the filings in front of me at the moment. If we can have the break now and I -- we can come back after the break and I can address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And I just noted there is a filing from the Prosecution for the extension of word limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any objection to that but we do -- I think there was possibly a misunderstanding with what you ordered. There is no reason for the motions themselves to be confidential. The annexes can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- be provisionally confidential. But I think the Registry has made everything confidential, which is, I don't believe, in keeping with what you ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the fault is on me. That can be cleared up very soon. We will break for 25 minutes and resume at five to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Ben Cerini, a legal intern who will be joining us for this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, there are three additional topics I would like to address; that's the Trnopolje camp, the Omarska camp, and a bit of the aftermath of your presence in Omarska camp. I'll try to do that efficiently as possible and focus my questions as well as I am able. First of all, you've discussed to some extent your period in hiding. At some point, did you make an effort to go to the vicinity of and ultimately attempt to enter Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for what purpose did you want to get inside Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The reason to get close to Trnopolje camp was my plan to leave the area, go via Trnopolje, Ribnjak and then Grmec. I certainly had to get close to Trnopolje in order to make that journey. When I got close to it, I observed the camp for two days, from a distance, and also what was going on in the camp. How the guard shifts went. It was quite far away, so I couldn't see everything, but I did see this area from where I could see things close-up, as it were. I did that because I was very close to the camp, and I noticed that the situation was such that I could enter the camp unobserved, and in this way, come to know what their plans were with these people. So that's what I did. After two or three days in the camp, six persons were killed who were in my immediate vicinity and who gave me some kind of assistance. That night around 2.00 a.m., I decided to leave. So I left the camp the same way I got in, and I went further away. However, I stayed nearby, though. The second time I got in was when I saw that many empty trucks and buses were getting close to Trnopolje. I decided to go in again because my impression was that an evacuation of the entire camp was being prepared. So I wanted to avail myself of that opportunity, to be evacuated as part of that group of women, children, et cetera. When I went in the second time, it wasn't really any kind of large-scale evacuation. Actually, the camp command had found out that I had been there. They detained about 15 people who had contact with me, and on pain of death, they asked about my whereabouts. Without knowing that, I entered the camp, and then I found out from someone that that was the case and, therefore, in order to save their lives, I surrendered, feeling that was the end of my own life. I sent one of these 15 men to call the camp commander so that I could surrender, and that's indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that -- you mentioned six persons who were killed after two or three days that you were in Trnopolje the first time. Can you tell the Court the names of those six persons who were killed, please.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Three families of brothers, all of them are Foric. All three families were made up two brothers respectively. There was a very young man among them and the oldest one there was a pensioner. They had no special reason. A uniformed soldier came who was a former neighbour of theirs, spoke to one of them briefly, and then, after a while, a policeman came with that soldier, and after that, they called out these men's names. They took them away. A few gun-shots were heard, and a few bursts of gun-fire, but in the morning we found out what had happened because a man from camp was taken away to bury the corpses. When he returned, he -- they asked him who they -- he buried, so he described the six of them, that one had Adidas sneakers, the other one had worker's overalls on and so on. My impression was that all of this happened to them on my account, and that is why I decided to leave the camp yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
