utterances.text: And do you know whether the bodies of the Forics have been exhumed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies of the Forics were found in a mass grave. The exhumation took place, I think, last year or the year before last, and now they are buried in the area of Kamicani, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court the general conditions in Trnopolje camp, food, medical care, sanitation facilities, security of persons there and so on?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There was no serious organisation except for the military organisation that supervised the camp. There was a shortage of food. There was no medical care whatsoever. Medical care was improvised by some medical men. Rather, a physician and a vet, a lady. Both of them were non-Serbs. They happened to be in the camp, and they were trying to help people. As for food, the camp authorities allowed a small group of people to leave the camp with proper approval to go back to their homes, to find remaining food supplies, like potatoes and flour, and to bring that back and thus feed people in the camp. As for military installations in the camp zone, there were some there. There were machine-gun nests, military check-points. There was a machine-gun nest on the house opposite the camp. There were guard posts, military guard posts. And they changed guards every two hours. They went around the camp. And I know all of that because I was observing all of this because I wanted to know at which point I could get out of a particular zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned what happened to the Forics. Can you tell us whether you became aware that others in camp were in physical jeopardy; and, if so, of what sort?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is the way it was: I heard that there had been a few killings. An old man had been killed. A woman. A youngish man. Out of the 15 persons I already mentioned, I heard about the ways in which they had been mistreated and beaten up, so that they would reveal where it was that I had been hiding although they did not really know. In the zone of the camp, or in the immediate vicinity of the camp, rapes took place in certain houses. Rapes were committed in the former cinema. That was one of the rooms within the camp itself. Younger women and children -- and -- and other women were taken in the area of Ribnjak and that's where rapes were committed as well. Also, there were killings in the area around the camp. There -- certain persons were wounded too. I know that a lady neighbour of mine was wounded in this way because see went to her vegetable garden to get some potatoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that some people were allowed to leave to get food. Was the camp enclosed by walls or wires or fencing?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the camp was surrounded by barbed wire. In a certain part, there was barbed wire even before the war but in this situation it was reinforced. There was yet another part that was completely open. However, there were military check-points there with machine-guns. The machine-guns were pointed at the area that did not have a fence. As for the roads, all around the camp there were military check-points, on all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that you sent someone to call the camp commander so that you could -- could surrender, and that's what happened. Who was that camp commander?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic. A man who attended the meeting when we were faced with an ultimatum. At the moment when he saw me, he said, This is not Sejmenovic. I know Sejmenovic. It was only when I spoke up, he said, Oh, is that you? Well, look at the way you look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where were you taken after your surrender to Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There was a brief interrogation at the camp command in Trnopolje. After that, they took me in the direction of Prijedor. They kept me for about 20 minutes at the military police building which was opposite the Keraterm camp. From there, they took me to the police station in Prijedor. There was a brief interrogation there. Of course, I was beaten up there. After that questioning, I was taken to the prison cell that was next to the dormitory of the special police or the Red Berets. Most of them came from Serbia. I was beaten rather severely there, because I was unconscious for a while. I was thrown into a cell where there were two women and two elderly men from Gomjenica or, rather, Cele.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the police station; and where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Two nights at the police station. After the second night, in the morning, or, rather, late in the morning, they took me to Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Upon arrival in Omarska camp, to what part of the camp were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The bus stopped right by the management building of the mine. As I was getting off the bus, I saw large groups of people right next to the bus, totally exhausted, malnourished, with bruises due to beatings. They were out there on an asphalt area and it was very hot outside. They all had to sit in the same position and all of them had their knees curled up close to them and that is how they sat in these regular squares right next to each other. And these areas were marked by chains, so they were chained off, like in a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you mentioned your questioning at the police station. Were you interrogated at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the interrogator question you about the number of weapons that Muslims had and where they were?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't question me about that. The first sentence was, "We are not interested in Prijedor. We are not interested in weapons. We know that you did not have any weapons. You had just a bit. But that is minor." End of quote. We are interested in Sarajevo. And then his interrogation started. He started interrogating me about what I remembered from Sarajevo, especially what I remembered and what I knew about Vitomir Zepinic and Miodrag Simovic. Later on, I was asked to say what I knew about Fikret Abdic, whether I had any contact with him and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the interrogator, do you know whether he was associated with any particular organ of the Bosnian Serb authorities or did you even know the interrogator himself?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The inspector was from the Prijedor police. He had come from the police building. He went out when I went out and he took the same bus to Omarska. He and two women who were secretaries at the Prijedor police station. Later on I saw that they worked in camp like secretaries as well. On the third day of the interrogation, he had announced that inspectors from Banja Luka would come to interrogate me. On that one day, there were these two inspectors from Banja Luka. People I saw for the first time on that day. They said that they were from Banja Luka. They attended the interrogation. They put a few questions but more or less the questions that had been put by Radakovic as well. They did not stay there long. Perhaps an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Radakovic. Is that the interrogator who questioned you first?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Dragan Radakovic, director of the Kozara National Park. He had a master's degree in psychology and he had a university degree in sculpture. He had introduced himself to me and said that we were supposed to be colleagues had there not been a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Court who guarded and secured the camp and how it was secured? Police, military, others, both, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part it was the military. When the bus approached Omarska, when we got off the main road between Prijedor and Banja Luka, that is to say, as we got to the road leading to Omarska itself there was a check-point with soldiers. The other check-point with soldiers was right by the railroad in Omarska and that is the road that leads to the camp or, rather, the industrial zone of the mine that later on became a camp. Some -- at some point halfway, near the mine installations, there was yet another military check-point, and in camp itself there were a few places where there was a concentration of soldiers. They were marching up and down the area where the prisoners were. Also, they were in the cafeteria area. There was just this glass house that the soldiers were not supposed to enter. This was a room between two areas that did not have a roof or ceiling but it had glass on two or three sides. Within the camp, there were also some men wearing classical police uniforms. The colour was blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you alluded at the beginning of your description of Omarska to the conditions of prisoners. Can you briefly describe for the Court, please, the conditions of prisoners and the conditions that prevailed in the camp with respect to the treatment of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Terrible. Not a single element that you could describe was not humane. Those who were brought in were beaten immediately. They ordered some inmates to beat up other inmates. They forced people to eat the one meal that they gave us for a very short time so that people were eating on the run. They didn't have enough time to eat this one piece of bread so they would put it into their chest so that they would eat the soup. People were beaten up all the time. On the PA, very loudly, they played Serbian nationalist songs all the time. And everywhere among groups of people you could see those who had been beaten up. Very often people had to be carried to the meal because they were not able to walk. The most awful scene I saw, which still haunts me, was of that a boy who was around 13 and whose both arms had been freshly broken. Both of them above his elbows and the right one also below the elbow. He couldn't eat. Those who were older than him carried him into the mess to take his piece of bread. They tried to feed him two or three spoonfuls, and then they would carry him back. They began interrogating this child the same day that they interrogated me. They forced him for one hour to sing Serbian songs which he didn't know. It was inhumane and pitiless machinery, which did not see anything human in anyone. It was turned only to itself. That was Omarska. Your Honour, I apologise, but this is a moment that -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, not at all. You don't have to apologise, Mr. Sejmenovic. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to show you a video. And as it is being set up - that's 40526A - I wanted to ask you quickly if you learned at some point that prisoners from Omarska had been transferred to Manjaca camp? Just yes or no, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that later, not at the Omarska camp but in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could briefly show 40526A. That's -- the transcript has been provided to the booth and we would be -- we don't need to identify the particular page. It's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Reporter: The Serb offer to release all prisoners into the hands of the Red Cross presents the civilised world with a sharp dilemma. If they're left in the camps, the prisoners face the threat of continuing humiliation, torture and death, but taking the prisoners away would help the Serbs in their war aim: Clearing Bosnia of Muslims and Croats. Privately, one Red Cross official calls it blackmail. Although while negotiations continue, public comments are more diplomatic. "Woman: You cannot only open doors and let them go. You have to be absolutely sure these people can go in safety with security guarantees and with a place to go. "Reporter: The exact terms of the offer to release prisoners are unclear. In one breath today, the Serbian leader Radovan Karadzic offered to close all camps, but in another, he spoke of releasing only prisoners of war too ill to go back into battle. "Karadzic: We don't have people in prisons that have been removed from their own homes. Those people have been captured in the battle-field, and they can go home if they are weak and they are not likely to -- to be mobilised from Muslim forces very soon."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With reference to this video, which is dated the 20th of August, 1992, can you indicate to the Court the extent to which the condition of these prisoners reflects the condition of or does not reflect the condition of the prisoners you saw at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It completely reflects their condition, though I had the chance to see even some worse cases than those we can see here. But even in this video we see an elderly man who is probably dying. This is what you can see in the video-clip. We see people who are malnourished, who have been beaten up. We see persons of various ages, from youngsters to old men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 40526A, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder whether this was Manjaca, where the witness was not held, and we will have witnesses from Manjaca. So I wonder why do it through this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was asked about similarity, and I said that I could observe similarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the exhibit number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 40526 -- oh, I'm sorry, the exhibit number. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, that's P3695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, were you present in Omarska when international journalists arrived?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you made available or offered to them by the Omarska officials to speak to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did not ask me anything. They just took me and brought me before the foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the foreign journalists speak to you and -- well, did the foreign journalists speak to you, first?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. When they saw me, they categorically refused to speak with me. They literally said, We won't speak with him. And the woman who was the interpreter interpreted that to them. And after that, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know why they wouldn't speak to you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Because, first of all, I was not brought to them on the drilling ground or the glass house but in the administrative building, where I had been brought previously. And, secondly, it was clear that that was manipulation with one of the inmates. In this case, it was manipulation with me. That was clear to the foreign journalists, and they gave up talking to me. Though, frankly speaking, I really wanted to address them because I saw a hope for my survival in this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you interviewed in Omarska by Bosnian Serb or Serbian journalists?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Twice. On the previous days. There was journalist Mutic who came and talked with me, told me what I should say if I wanted to save my life and left. He promised that he would bring a written text that I would read for him into the camera. Two days later, as far as I remember, he came with the text and I did read the text into the camera in the manner in which I believed it was necessary for me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what organisation was Mutic from?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Mutic was SDS personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did he work for any particular media outlet or agency?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Mutic worked for the "Kozarski Vjesnik" and for Radio Prijedor and he was also the official cameraman of the 5th Kozara Brigade while it was conducting war operations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you also interviewed by journalists from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Not from Serbia but there were Serbian journalists from Sarajevo, or, rather, from Pale. They interviewed me. It was Dragan Bozanic [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnic"] who interviewed me. He was a journalist of SRNA at the time. I think that was the name of their news agency. And he conducted interview with me in one of the offices at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me show you a video next, 65 ter 40504A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's page 4 of the English for the interpreters' booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And while we are waiting, Mr. Sejmenovic, the transcript says Dragan Bosnic. Was it Bosnic or another name?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Bozanic, B-o-z-a-n-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ERN on the English transcript is 03065658.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The Serb offer to release all prisoners into the hands of the Red Cross presents the civilised --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... nor were they interested in the hospital of this centre. They were interested in Mevludin Sejmenovic who was an activist within this area. "We heard that you are one of the few inmates of this reception centre here" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe we can stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Sejmenovic, did you have a chance to see the person interviewing you; and can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is the former journalists of the radio and television of Bosnia and Herzegovina who was a journalist of the Serbian television from Pale in this period, and that is Dragan Bozanic about whom I have been talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the record just to indicate we stopped at 838.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, during the course of that interview, were you asked about -- to -- to talk about the actions or activities of other SDA leaders, about priests and -- excuse me, hodzas, that is, Muslim priests, and other matters?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Bozanic, as documented in this video-clip, asked me almost identical questions as journalist Mutic several days earlier, and Mutic was a journalist of the local media. So everything I was asked here I had mostly already been asked by journalist Mutic in -- on the previous occasion when a statement was taken from me. And I answered in the manner in which I was told to do because they told me that in that way I could save my own life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The interview includes such questions and comments as condemning Mirza Mujadzic as someone to blame for all the horror that happened here in this region, and also refers to evidence of Muslim hodzas engaged in arming or smuggling in some other way. Were those things true; and, if not, why did you say them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: These things were absolutely incorrect. But that was the only thing that I could say and that I was requested to say so that I would not jeopardise my own life. If I had told the truth, I would probably have ended my life an hour after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn quickly to one more clip on that video, 4054B is this clip. Page 7 of the English for the interpreters' booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are not able to find this on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe it begins at the very bottom of page 6 and essentially begins at the top of page 7.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, do you recognise the journalist speaking there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is the same journalist, Dragan Bozanic. The one we already talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the record I stopped that at 15.49.9, after we -- after the camera panned past the journalist. If we can keep going just a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We wish to live on -- live here still, not to leave our homesteads. So you should report about that. "And which government? There are many governments ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the journalist shown on the other side of the wire here? And that's at 16.01.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The one with the beard could be Mutic. It shows him in profile, so I'm slightly reserved but I think that it is Mutic because he is bald and because he has a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, does this depict interviews conducted at a portion of the Trnopolje camp that you've referred to earlier, with the wire?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender 40504A and B, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibits P3696 and P3697, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, at around the time that the international journalists arrived, did you also see any high-level Republika Srpska officials come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were several important local officials. They were there on the same day when the journalists came. Some of them arrived earlier and others at the same time as the journalists. And then on the following day, an official of the Autonomous Region of Krajina also came. That was Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you learn -- first of all, did Kupresanin speak to you, and did you have occasion to learn why he came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The guards took me from the glass house to the administrative building, to the top floor. I didn't know the reason until an elderly greying man appeared. I believed that this was someone from the municipal assembly in Prijedor but he introduced himself by saying, I'm Vojo Kupresanin. And then, of course, I recalled that that was Kupresanin, though it looked unbelievable. He told me that he wished to talk with me. He told me to sit down. I sat on another chair, and we had this conversation which was mostly Kupresanin's monologue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now -- and -- and did you learn eventually whether Kupresanin wanted to take you out of the camp; and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the middle of this conversation, he was called to the office next door. It was actually across the corridor from ours, with an open door. A soldier called him and told him, The president needs you. I think he said the president. Kupresanin responded and he told him, he told him, the one who called, the president, that he needed 300 beds and 300 soap bars urgently. At least that number. He talked about that and he also said something to the effect, I only found one. I thought that referred to me but I wasn't sure. Briefly after that, I learned that he actually meant me, and that -- and he told me that I would be leaving for Banja Luka with him now. He took me out. We got into a car and we started for Banja Luka. During the ride to Banja Luka he asked me whether there were any other deputies who were alive. Where was Mujadzic, where was Senad Cero [phoen]. He said we should collect them. This is what he said. He asked me about my family members and so on and so forth. It was only later, a few hours later, and completely a day or two afterwards, that I learned what exactly were Kupresanin's intentions and what was the reason why he had taken me away from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how did you learn that and what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Part of it I learned from him because he was saying I need to get better, to fatten up, that he would place me with a Serb -- a Serb village, Kukuruzari, but I heard him talking to another man on the phone to whom he said he had found me. He received some instructions and he said in response he was already planning to get me a suit, to allow me time to get better. And then he said that he was planning to organise some round-table discussions with me so that I could make a public appearance, speaking about the situation in Bosnian Krajina. But I learned the rest of it from the driver who was taking me to Vrbanija, to the house of my sister who lived up there. And the driver said, I quote: It's good for you that you decided to be a member of the Serbian Assembly, except somebody will kill you for it. You must not go around Vrbanija. You must not leave the house because the extremists would kill you otherwise. I was not in a position where I could comment or respond to any of this. I just took notice of what I had heard and kept thinking about my situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two questions. The man that Kupresanin was speaking to in that second phone call, were you able to identify who that man was from what Kupresanin said or from any other aspect of the phone call?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Kupresanin said that in so many words after the conversation, and I'd heard the voice of Mr. Karadzic that was very familiar to me from all the sessions. Because it was the old-fashioned type of telephone set, and the desk on which the telephone sat was not far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, second question, you referred to Kupresanin speaking to the person he called president or who was -- he was called to as president. That he needed 300 beds and 300 soap bars urgently. Can you tell the Court whether you were able in -- at that time to form any impression about why Kupresanin needed those items or was requesting those items; that is, was it for the -- out of any particular concerns for the prisoners or other reasons? Whatever you were able to deduce.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speculation. Speculation. The question calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second. No, just a second. As far as witness can answer the question, he is able to -- he is entitled to answer. Please proceed, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that part of the conversation in Omarska. A part of the conversation I heard after the filming made by foreign crews of reporters. I did not see any particular concern about the conduct within the camp. And as for Kupresanin, he did not express any feelings about the situation in the camp. During that brief conversation we had, he spoke to me about international politics and that's what he elaborated on. That it was a conspiracy of the Vatican and the Comintern to portray Serbs as executioners of Muslims, and he was talking in a monologue. I had no courage to get involved, really, in that conversation or to debate him because of the position I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, you spoke about the -- what you understood to be the intentions for you based on those discussions and conversations. At some point, were you asked to -- well, first of all, let me set the stage a little bit back. After this, were you taken to Vrbanija to stay?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was at my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at some point during the period while you were there, were you told by Mr. Kupresanin that you were to come to Banja Luka to meet Mr. Karadzic and also, perhaps, some members of a high-level international delegation that were visiting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Kupresanin came to Vrbanija twice. Once -- sorry, no, he came three times. Once, when he came, he wanted to take me to some place to convince the Territorial Defence of Kotor Varos to surrender. I refused that, explaining my reasons. Another time he came saying that he was planning to drive me to Bihac, to the separation line, for me to be a member of the Serbian negotiating team discussing some military issues. And the third time he came, he said I have very little time, to get dressed, that I am to see Karadzic in Banja Luka and -- not only Karadzic but some other people as well. And that's his third visit to Vrbanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me quickly show you 45389.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I invited Mr. Vance and Lord Owen to come to Banja Luka to see for themselves if that is indeed so; namely, whenever there is a favourable course to the conference and when the course is favourable for us, then it happens that some sort of lies are put out by the Muslim circles, either that people are being killed in a bread line or that Sarajevo is being bombed. Sarajevo, they themselves are bombing Sarajevo. "Moderator: It is fact that the world is beginning to grasp more and more what it is all about. "Karadzic: Yes. For the most part these tricks are quite transparent. However, Vance and Owen wanted to come and see and I invited them, and we met them in Bosanska Gradiska, took them around. People welcomed them very warmly. There was an entire programme for their stay in Banja Luka. They requested to see the people. Some people they wanted to see. There were many Muslims there. There were two officials of the Party for Democratic Action which is not banned in Republika Srpska even though -- yes, in the territories where the Muslims dominate. They were able to speak to all of them in private. "They also received religious leaders, prelates from Krajina of all of the three denominations. Then they talked with municipal officials. They assured themselves President Radic is a very exceptional person, a man who rules that city, governs that city according to the law. They also saw the chief of police, Zupljanin. They could see for themselves that the authorities there are doing everything they can so that the tensions do not flare up, that those tensions that necessarily exist because of this war do not result in any sort of evacuation. They assured themselves of these things. They even publicly said that Banja Luka is still not affected by ethnic cleansing although the tensions run high. "We showed them documentation from which one can see that a secret Muslim organisation does exist there. That even one wing of the Merhamet organisation is trading in arms and that this secret organisation whose members we know, all of them, and we are monitoring their work, wants to create chaos in Banja Luka, but that they are, however, waiting for the European Community monitors to arrive. And that is why we are postponing the arrival of the EC monitors. It might not even be necessary for them to come as their arrival would cause chaos. "It's a fact this did happen in Krajina, that some people left the areas but not from Banja Luka. It happened, for example, after one ambush between Petrovac and Bihac where 16 Serbs were killed. Not killed but slaughtered. Then there was another ambush in which three Serbs were killed, and in that clash, 11 Muslims were killed and 19 Serbs in total. Then the families of the Muslims fighting in Alija's army or in the official army wanted to leave Petrovac although they were being dissuaded from this by officials. They left Petrovac anyway and went somewhere to Central Bosnia. "And I would be happy if the Muslim side would let the Serbs go. And they will have to let them go according to the papers we signed in Geneva. The Serbs from Sarajevo to go from one city, one part of the city to another, or the Serbs from Tuzla about whom we are very concerned and whom we shall demand to be allowed out of Zenica, Travnik and all the other places under Muslim control. "Simply they had to say, Lord Owen has even publically said that this has not spread to Banja Luka, that there are tensions, but that we are in the middle of a civil war and Banja Luka is a happy place where children play in the streets. There is even a police force, including Muslims and Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, a couple of quick questions and we will be able to complete today. First of all, the -- do you understand the event that's being depicted here that is -- and referred to here? That is, the invitation of Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen to come to Banja Luka to relate to the visit that Kupresanin had you make to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. On the day before last, I heard that these two high international officials were supposed to come to Banja Luka, and when Kupresanin came that morning to say that I was going to see Mr. Karadzic and other people, I inferred that those other people were precisely those international negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, second, there's a reference to two functionaries of the Party of Democratic Action. Did you understand you were one of the -- that you were an SDA functionary who was supposed to go to Banja Luka to meet those international officials?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly I was one of the two. Now, who the others are, I don't know. Why do I say that I don't know? Because I was taken to that building where this conference, this meeting, was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Sejmenovic, when Mr. Karadzic referred to people in the Krajina leaving and that those were families of Muslims fighting in Alija's army who wanted to leave, is that kind of departure of Muslims consistent with what you observed of the circumstances in which Muslims were -- that Muslims left areas of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry but I have to say this again. Apart from the fact that these two men, Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, really arrived, the rest is complete manipulation and a travesty of what was going on there. What was going on was exactly the opposite of what is described here. This is the kind of pamphlet propaganda that we had so many occasions to see even before these events and after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time but I only have two small clips -- one small clip and one quick document I think I can finish within five minutes with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes with the indulgence of staff we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My appreciation to the staff. If we could turn quickly to 65 ter 45064. And for the interpreter's booth, that's the last paragraph on that page you should have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "'We were not deluded,' Associated Press quoted Vance as saying upon his arrival in Zagreb from Banja Luka. He added, 'We heard some rumours, we went there and it's been confirmed, so we know that this is happening in the region,' AP reports. "Following talks with Radovan Karadzic, Vance told reporters that he could not agree with the Bosnian Serb leader who said that no ethnic cleansing was taking place here. And that Owen and himself should verify certain matters before making up their minds, as well as that his impression was that the situation was much worse than they had expected, AP reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sejmenovic, when Mr. Vance disputes what Mr. Karadzic says and says there was ethnic cleansing, is that consistent with your observations of what was taking place in the region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It is consistent, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender both those video-clips, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P3698 and P3699, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Sejmenovic, is it correct that you were finally able to leave the area in January of 1993? That is, the area of Vrbanija and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I left on the 15th of January, 1992 -- sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you have to obtain a number of documents to present to the international agencies in order to do so? To the international agencies, as well as various officials.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I had to have an ID. I did not have an ID, so I tried to get hold of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we turn to 65 ter 20155, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is that one of the documents that you obtained?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Right. That's the document with the only photo that I had at the time, and that's my picture from the army, when I was 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3700, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that concludes my examination-in-chief, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I hear from Ms. Sutherland briefly about the point you raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In relation to the supplemental memorandum -- well, actually, does the witness still need to be here or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do it tomorrow given the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can do that, Your Honour. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll rise for today and resume tomorrow at the same time, i.e., 2.15. Mr. Sejmenovic, you may be aware of this, but while your testimony is going on, you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I will abide by the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I did want to mention that in relation Mr. Karadzic's motion for the admission of public redacted version of Exhibit D01523, we don't oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of October, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m.,
